title: FACIAL CLEFTING, OBLIQUE, 1
alt_titles: OCULOMAXILLOFACIAL DYSPLASIA WITH OBLIQUE FACIAL CLEFTS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by loss-of-function mutation in the SPECC1L gene.

checks.claim: Oblique facial clefting-1 (OBLFC1) is caused by loss-of-function mutation in the SPECC1L gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We show that loss-of-function mutations in SPECC1L are pathogenic for this human developmental disorder
checks.explanation: Abstract states LOF SPECC1L mutations are pathogenic for ObFC; OBLFC1 naming is nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Oblique facial clefts are rare facial malformations. Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) stated that they include types 2 to 6 of the Tessier classification. Saadi et al. (2011) described oblique facial clefts as a unique class of facial malformations.

paragraphs.text: Tessier (1976) proposed an anatomical classification of facial, craniofacial, and laterofacial clefts. He based it on personal observations and used the orbit as the primary structure of reference. The classification distinguished 15 cleft locations and described the course of each through soft tissue and bone. Tessier (1976) also discussed combinations of several cleft types and associated malformations. Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) noted that oblique facial clefts include types 2 to 6 of this classification.

paragraphs.text: Richieri-Costa and Gorlin (1994) reported 4 Brazilian patients with oblique facial clefts who had a strikingly similar facial appearance. Three of the 4 patients had consanguineous parents. The authors suggested that the pattern of facial involvement and the overall clinical picture pointed to a unique dysmorphogenetic process. They also suggested that in some cases the condition could represent an oculomaxillofacial dysostosis.

paragraphs.text: In a girl with bilateral oblique facial clefts, Dasouki et al. (1988) found a de novo balanced translocation between chromosome 1 and chromosome 22 on peripheral blood karyotype. They noted that a submicroscopic imbalance resulting from the translocation could not be ruled out. They recommended chromosome studies in children with such rare malformations.

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) showed that loss-of-function mutations in the SPECC1L gene are pathogenic for oblique facial clefts. In functional studies, SPECC1L deficiency caused defective reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and abnormal cell adhesion and migration. Knockdown of SPECC1L homologs in zebrafish and Drosophila also produced abnormal phenotypes (see ANIMAL MODEL).

paragraphs.text: Saadi et al. (2011) found that during mouse embryogenesis, Specc1l is expressed in the cells of the developing facial primordia, which proliferate and fuse to form the face. In mammalian cells, SPECC1L colocalized with both tubulin and actin. SPECC1L deficiency caused defective reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and abnormal cell adhesion and migration. The authors concluded that SPECC1L functions in reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton and is required for proper facial morphogenesis.
